The single thing to watch while marking: **did the student reverse the arrow for every "necessary"?**
A script with no backwards arrows anywhere has mistranslated the word, whatever the final answers say.

# Section A — Fluency

## Question 1 **[4]**

::: {.question}
$P,Q$ statements. Write each as an implication. &nbsp;&nbsp;(a) $Q$ is **sufficient** for $P$. &nbsp;
(b) $Q$ is **necessary** for $P$. &nbsp; (c) A **necessary** condition for $P$ is $Q$. &nbsp; (d) Which
**two** of (a)–(c) say the same thing?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Answer

**(a)** $Q \Rightarrow P$ &nbsp; **(B1)** &nbsp; *— sufficient points forwards, from $Q$.*

**(b)** $P \Rightarrow Q$ &nbsp; **(B1)** &nbsp; *— necessary points backwards, so the arrow starts at $P$.*

**(c)** $P \Rightarrow Q$ &nbsp; **(B1)**

*Target is $P$ (it follows "condition **for**"), condition is $Q$, rule is necessary: target $\Rightarrow$
condition, i.e. $P \Rightarrow Q$.*

**(d) (b) and (c)** — both are $P \Rightarrow Q$. &nbsp; **(B1)**

**Marking note.** (b) and (c) are the same statement written two ways; if a student has them different,
the reversed wording in (c) is what tripped them, not the word *necessary*.
:::

---

## Question 2 **[3]**

::: {.question}
$n$ a positive integer. For each pair, is the first **sufficient / necessary / both / neither** for the
second (justify)? &nbsp;&nbsp;(a) "$n$ divisible by $9$" · "$n$ divisible by $3$"; &nbsp; (b) "$n$ divisible
by $3$" · "$n$ divisible by $9$"; &nbsp; (c) "$n$ divisible by $2$ and by $5$" · "$n$ divisible by $10$".
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Answer

**(a) Sufficient, but not necessary.** &nbsp; **(B1)**

- Forwards: if $9$ divides $n$ then $n = 9k = 3(3k)$, so $3$ divides $n$. ✓
- Backwards: $n = 3$ is divisible by $3$ but not by $9$. ✗

**(b) Necessary, but not sufficient.** &nbsp; **(B1)** &nbsp; *— the mirror image of (a); same
counterexample $n=3$.*

**(c) Both.** &nbsp; **(B1)**

- Forwards: if $2$ divides $n$ and $5$ divides $n$, then since $2, 5$ share no factor, $10$ divides $n$. ✓
- Backwards: if $10$ divides $n$ then $n = 10k = 2(5k) = 5(2k)$. ✓

**Award (a) and (b) only if both directions were addressed** — a verdict of "sufficient" with no
backwards test is a guess that happened to land.
:::

---

## Question 3 **[3]**

::: {.question}
Write each as an implication between $P$ and $Q$. &nbsp;&nbsp;(a) For $P$ to hold it is **necessary** that
$Q$ holds. &nbsp; (b) A **sufficient** condition for $P$ is $Q$. &nbsp; (c) $P$ is **necessary and
sufficient** for $Q$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Answer

**(a)** $P \Rightarrow Q$ &nbsp; **(B1)** &nbsp; *— "for $P$ … necessary that $Q$": target $P$, condition
$Q$, so target $\Rightarrow$ condition.*

**(b)** $Q \Rightarrow P$ &nbsp; **(B1)** &nbsp; *— target $P$, condition $Q$, sufficient, so condition
$\Rightarrow$ target.*

**(c)** $P \Leftrightarrow Q$ &nbsp; **(B1)**

*Note (a) and (b) are converses of each other — the same two letters, opposite arrows, purely because one
says necessary and the other sufficient.*
:::

# Section B — Exam standard

## Question 4 **[5]**

::: {.question}
Let $x$ be real and $T$ the target $x^3>8$. For each condition, is it **sufficient / necessary / both /
neither** for $T$ (justify)? &nbsp;&nbsp;(a) $x>2$; &nbsp; (b) $x>3$; &nbsp; (c) $x>0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Answer

For real $x$, cubing preserves order, so $\;x^3 > 8 \iff x > 2$. &nbsp; **(M1 for recognising this)**

**(a) $x>2$: both — necessary and sufficient.** &nbsp; **(A1)**

It is *exactly* the target, by the line above.

**(b) $x>3$: sufficient, but not necessary.** &nbsp; **(A1)**

- Forwards: $x>3 \Rightarrow x>2 \Rightarrow x^3>8$. ✓
- Backwards: $x = 2.5$ gives $x^3 = 15.625 > 8$, but $x \not> 3$. ✗

**(c) $x>0$: necessary, but not sufficient.** &nbsp; **(B1)**

- Backwards: $x^3>8 \Rightarrow x>2 \Rightarrow x>0$. ✓ necessary.
- Forwards: $x = 1$ gives $x^3 = 1 \not> 8$. ✗ not sufficient.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Contrast this with the class material's Question 6**, where the target was $x^2>4$ and the negative
branch broke necessity. **Cubes have no negative branch** — $x^3>8$ really does mean just $x>2$ — so the
usual "check the negatives" habit finds nothing here. Worth saying aloud: the habit is to *check*, not to
assume there is always a second branch.
:::
:::

## Question 5 **[5]**

::: {.question}
$n$ a positive integer; $(*)$: *if $n$ is divisible by $6$ then $n$ is even*. Which, taken individually,
is/are equivalent to $(*)$? &nbsp;&nbsp;**I** a necessary condition for $n$ to be even is that $n$ is
divisible by $6$; &nbsp; **II** $n$ divisible by $6$ is sufficient for $n$ even; &nbsp; **III** if $n$ is
odd then $n$ is not divisible by $6$. &nbsp; (Options **A**–**H**.)
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Answer — **F** (II and III)

Let $P$ = "$n$ is divisible by $6$", $Q$ = "$n$ is even". Then $(*) = P \Rightarrow Q$.
&nbsp; **(M1 for naming and the arrow)**

**I.** "A **necessary** condition **for $n$ to be even**"— target $Q$, condition $P$, rule necessary, so
target $\Rightarrow$ condition:
$$Q \Rightarrow P .$$
That is the **converse**. **Not equivalent** ✗ — and also false ($n=2$ is even, not divisible by $6$).
&nbsp; **(B1)**

**II.** "$P$ is **sufficient** for $Q$" is $P \Rightarrow Q$ — that is $(*)$ itself. **Equivalent** ✓
&nbsp; **(B1)**

**III.** "If $n$ is odd, then $n$ is not divisible by $6$" is not $Q \Rightarrow$ not $P$ — the
**contrapositive**. **Equivalent** ✓ &nbsp; **(B1)**

**Answer: F.** &nbsp; **(A1)**

**Marking note.** Statement I is the trap, and it is a double one: the wording is reversed *and* the word
is *necessary*, so two mistranslations can cancel out and give the right arrow for the wrong reason. Check
the working, not just the letter.
:::

---

## Question 6 **[4]**

::: {.question}
$ABCD$ is a quadrilateral. &nbsp;&nbsp;(a) Why is "all four sides equal" a **necessary** condition for
$ABCD$ to be a square? &nbsp; (b) Show it is **not sufficient**. &nbsp; (c) State a **necessary and
sufficient** condition for $ABCD$ to be a square.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Answer

**(a)** Every square has four equal sides, so
$$(\text{square}) \Rightarrow (\text{four equal sides}) ,$$
and a condition implied *by* the target is exactly what **necessary** means. &nbsp; **(B1)**

**(b)** A **rhombus** that is not a square — for instance one with angles $60^\circ$ and $120^\circ$ — has
four equal sides but is not a square. &nbsp; **(M1 A1)**

*The condition holds and the target fails, so the condition does not guarantee the target: not sufficient.*

**(c)** Any correct characterisation, e.g. &nbsp; **(B1)**

- "all four sides equal **and** all four angles are right angles";
- "a rectangle with two adjacent sides equal";
- "a rhombus with one right angle".

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**The mark in (b) is for the example, not the explanation.** *"Four equal sides doesn't fix the angles"*
is the right thought, but the question says **show**, which means produce a specific shape where the
condition holds and the conclusion fails.
:::
:::

# Section C — Stretch

## Question 7 **[5]**

::: {.question}
$x^2+bx+1=0$ ($b$ real) is *good* if it has **two distinct real roots**. &nbsp;&nbsp;(a) Show it is good
iff $b^2>4$. &nbsp; (b) For each, is it **sufficient / necessary / both / neither** for the equation to be
good? &nbsp;(i) $b>2$; &nbsp;(ii) $\lvert b\rvert>2$; &nbsp;(iii) $b>0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Answer

**(a)** The equation has two distinct real roots exactly when its discriminant is positive:
$$b^2 - 4(1)(1) > 0 \iff b^2 > 4 . \qquad \textbf{(B1)}$$

**(b)** Note $b^2 > 4 \iff |b| > 2 \iff (b>2 \text{ or } b<-2)$.

**(i) $b>2$: sufficient, but not necessary.** &nbsp; **(M1 A1)**

- Forwards: $b>2 \Rightarrow b^2>4$. ✓
- Backwards: $b = -3$ gives $b^2 = 9 > 4$ (good), but $b \not> 2$. ✗

**(ii) $|b|>2$: both.** &nbsp; **(A1)** — it is precisely the condition from part (a).

**(iii) $b>0$: neither.** &nbsp; **(A1)**

- Not sufficient: $b = 1$ gives $b^2 = 1 \not> 4$. ✗
- Not necessary: $b = -3$ is good but not positive. ✗

*Here the squares warning does apply — the negative branch $b < -2$ is what breaks necessity in both (i)
and (iii).*
:::

## Question 8 **[3]**

::: {.question}
$A,B$ statements. &nbsp;&nbsp;(a) Given $A$ is necessary for $B$ **and** $A$ is sufficient for $B$, what
can you conclude about $A$ and $B$? &nbsp; (b) A student writes "*$A$ is necessary for $B$, so $B$ is
necessary for $A$*". Right? Justify.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Answer

**(a)** Necessary gives $B \Rightarrow A$ and sufficient gives $A \Rightarrow B$, so both arrows hold:
$$A \Leftrightarrow B .$$
$A$ and $B$ are **equivalent** — each is true in exactly the same circumstances as the other. &nbsp; **(B1)**

**(b) No, the student is wrong.** &nbsp; **(M1)**

- "$A$ is necessary for $B$" means $B \Rightarrow A$.
- "$B$ is necessary for $A$" means $A \Rightarrow B$.

These are **converses** of each other, and a converse does not follow from the original. &nbsp; **(A1)**

*Counterexample: let $A$ = "$n$ is even" and $B$ = "$n$ is divisible by $4$". Then $A$ is necessary for
$B$ (every multiple of $4$ is even), but $B$ is not necessary for $A$ ($n=2$ is even and not a multiple of
$4$).*

**Teaching point.** Swapping the two letters around "necessary" **reverses** the claim — exactly as
swapping them around "only if" did in Session 1. If both directions did happen to hold, that would be
part (a): equivalence, which has to be earned, never assumed.
:::

## Marking summary

| Q | Marks | The thing being tested |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 4 | Translating both words, including reversed wording |
| 2 | 3 | Testing **both** arrows before giving a verdict |
| 3 | 3 | Reversed wording again, at speed |
| 4 | 5 | Four verdicts on one target; cubes have no second branch |
| 5 | 5 | Equivalence under exam wording; the double-trap option I |
| 6 | 4 | **Showing "not sufficient" with an example**, not an explanation |
| 7 | 5 | Discriminant plus the four verdicts; the negative branch |
| 8 | 3 | Necessary in both directions = equivalence |

**If marks are lost in one place, look at Questions 1(c), 3 and 5(I).** All three use the reversed
*"a … condition for … is …"* wording, which is what the TMUA actually prints. A student who is fluent
with the plain form but stumbles on the reversed one will lose marks on nearly every real Paper 2
question in this topic.
:::
